---
title: "Quickselect"
description: "A detailed, example-first algorithm lesson connecting CLRS-style reasoning with LeetCode interview patterns."
---

## Start with the problem, not a formula

**LeetCode 215 — Kth Largest Element in an Array**. Use partitioning to locate an order statistic without fully sorting.

Imagine solving a tiny case by hand before writing any code. Ask what information you are recalculating unnecessarily and what information you could carry to the next decision.

## Why the obvious approach is expensive

Sorting the entire array costs n log n comparisons even though you only want one rank.

## Discover the key idea

Partition around a pivot. The pivot divides values into left and right regions; after partition, only ONE side can contain the requested rank.

This is the moment to explain the technique aloud, without using its name as a substitute for understanding.

## Mathematical model — then immediately translate it

$$
k<p\Rightarrow\text{search left};\quad k>p\Rightarrow\text{search right}
$$

**Explanation of every symbol:** k is the wanted zero-based sorted rank, p is the pivot's final sorted rank after a suitable partition; left/right refer to elements smaller/larger than the pivot.

**Substitute actual values:** Take [8,2,7,1,9] and ask for the middle value k=2 (the third smallest). If pivot 7 is placed at p=2, the answer is already 7. If pivot 2 ended at p=1, discard all elements at ranks ≤1 and search the right side.

Notice that the numbers come **immediately after the formula**. Reading the equation should lead to the same decision you would make with paper and pencil.

## Work through the algorithm

1. Identify the initial state using the small example above.
2. Make one legal decision and update only state affected by that decision.
3. Verify the invariant again. If it fails, correct the state before making another decision.
4. Repeat until the search space is exhausted or the answer has been justified.

**Why this is correct:** Partition establishes that elements left of the pivot are no larger and elements right are no smaller. Therefore the desired order statistic cannot be in the discarded side.

## Actual code — keep it small

The original [Node.js example library](../examples/patterns.mjs) implements this technique as `quickselect` and tests it against boundary cases:

~~~js
import { quickselect } from '../examples/patterns.mjs';

console.log(quickselect([8,2,7,1,9],2));
~~~

Save this snippet in the current topic folder as a `.mjs` file, then run it with Node. The function is tested with `node --test algorithms/examples/patterns.test.mjs` from repository root.

## Analyse the work; do not guess big-O

**Cost:** Expected O(n) time with suitable randomisation, worst-case O(n²) for naive pivoting; O(n) copied space in this educational implementation.

The important complexity question is which operation may repeat and how many times it can repeat. In a recursion, count the decision-tree branches; with pointers, count total forward movements; with graph searches, count visits to vertices and edges.

## Break the technique deliberately

A bad pivot can repeatedly leave size n−1 and yield O(n²) time. Randomised or carefully chosen pivots improve expected or worst-case guarantees. Duplicates require a correct partition scheme.

If the problem's assumptions change, return to the invariant and check whether it still holds. An algorithmic pattern is a consequence of assumptions, not a keyword to memorise.
